d1-1.ev: The 101st lands in daylight beside the museum as Operation Market Garden opens.

q.t: Why start the tour at this museum?
o: It explains the plan before you drive the road
q.x: It sits almost on Drop Zone B and explains the corridor plan before you drive the road.

d1-1.rem: The museum sits almost on Drop Zone B, the ground the 101st landed on.
d1-1.st: On 17 September 1944 the 101st landed on the ground where the Wings of Liberation Museum now stands, almost on Drop Zone B. The museum tells the story of the Brabant liberation with vehicles, aircraft and a Waco glider, and it explains the plan of Operation Market Garden before the corridor road is driven. That makes it the right place to start. Today the corridor map inside is the first thing to study.

d1-2.ev: The 506th jumps in daylight onto the heath in near-perfect order.

q.t: How did the 506th's drop into Holland compare with Normandy?
o: On target, assembled within the hour
q.x: In daylight, on target and with little flak, the company assembled within the hour, the best drop the regiment ever had.

d1-2.rem: The best drop the regiment ever had: daylight, on target, and the company together within the hour.
d1-2.st: Around 13:00 on 17 September 1944, Operation Market Garden opened in daylight and the 506th jumped onto this heath between Son and Best. It was the best drop the regiment ever had: on target, with little flak, and the company assembled within the hour. Compared with Normandy it was a parade. Today nothing marks the exact spot; the flat open ground itself, dry and wide, is the point.

d1-3.ev: The Germans blow the Wilhelmina Canal bridge as the 506th reaches it.

q.t: How did Easy cross the Wilhelmina Canal at Son?
o: On an engineers' footbridge at night
q.x: The Germans blew the bridge as the 506th arrived; engineers rigged a footbridge overnight and Easy crossed in the dark.

d1-3.rem: The blown bridge at Son cost the whole corridor a day.
d1-3.st: The Wilhelmina Canal bridge at Son was the 506th's first objective. As the lead battalion reached the canal on the afternoon of 17 September, the Germans blew the bridge, and an 88 mm gun on the far bank fired down the road. Engineers rigged a footbridge that night and Easy crossed in the dark; the delay cost the whole corridor a day. Today a 101st Airborne memorial stands on 17 Septemberplein beside the modern bridge.

d1-4.ev: The 506th enters Eindhoven from the north along this road through Woensel.

q.t: Who placed the Airborne Memorial on Airbornelaan?
q.x: 101st veterans placed it in 1969, on the road the 506th used to enter the city on 18 September.

d1-4.rem: The link-up with the British Second Army happened a few streets from here.
d1-4.st: On 18 September 1944 the 506th entered Eindhoven from the north through Woensel, along what is now Airbornelaan, and cleared the town by early afternoon. The Guards Armoured Division's tanks arrived that evening and the corridor was open, a day late; the link-up with the British Second Army happened a few streets from here. 101st veterans placed this memorial in 1969. Today its plaque stands on the road the regiment used.

d1-5.ev: Easy marches through cheering crowds; that night the Luftwaffe bombs the city.

q.t: How did Eindhoven's liberation-day celebrations end?
o: With a German counterattack at dawn
With a Luftwaffe bombing that night
q.x: Easy marched through cheering crowds on 18 September; that night the Luftwaffe bombed the city and the celebrations ended.

d1-5.rem: The square is named for liberation day, 18 September, a day of celebration that ended in bombing.
d1-5.st: This square is named for Eindhoven's liberation day. On 18 September 1944 Easy Company marched through cheering crowds here as the 506th cleared the town. That night the Luftwaffe bombed the city and the celebrations ended. The Philips town the paratroopers saw was largely rebuilt in the years that followed. Today the visitor walks a rebuilt centre, where only the square's name keeps the date.

d1-6.ev: Riding British tanks toward Helmond, Easy runs into the 107th Panzer Brigade.
d1-6.rem: A plaque here names nine Easy Company men who fell in Holland between 19 September and 5 October.
d1-6.st: On 19–20 September Easy Company rode east on British Cromwell tanks toward Helmond and ran into the 107th Panzer Brigade at the edge of Nuenen. Tanks were knocked out, the company was pinned and pulled back with about fifteen casualties, and Bull Randleman, missing, spent the night hiding in a barn. Beside the village liberation monument, a plaque names nine Easy men who fell in Holland. Today the road east toward Helmond crosses open fields without cover.

d1-7.ev: The corridor road runs through the 502nd's town on Hell's Highway.

q.t: Whose town was Sint-Oedenrode on the corridor?
q.x: It was the 502nd's town; the highway through it is the original road and shows how narrow the operation was.

d1-7.rem: One road, two ditches, flat fields either side: the whole operation depended on a road this narrow.
d1-7.st: Sint-Oedenrode was the 502nd's town on the corridor, and the highway through it is the original road. The whole operation depended on this single route, Hell's Highway, and here it is easy to feel how narrow that lifeline was. In the days after the landings the 101st fought again and again to keep it open. Today the visitor sees one road, two ditches and flat fields on either side.

d1-8.ev: The Germans attack the canal bridges; the 101st fights for two days to keep the road open.

q.t: Why was Veghel the corridor's most vulnerable point?
o: Four bridges over canal and river
q.x: Four bridges over the canal and the river made Veghel vulnerable; the Germans attacked on 22 September.

d1-8.rem: Every hour the road was shut here, the men at Arnhem were nearer defeat.
d1-8.st: Four bridges over the canal and the river made Veghel the corridor's most vulnerable point. The Germans attacked it on 22 September, and the 101st fought for two days to keep the road open. Every hour Hell's Highway was shut, the men at Arnhem were nearer defeat, so these crossings carried the fate of the whole operation. Today the bridges over the Zuid-Willemsvaart remain the objective everyone wanted.

d1-9.ev: Cut off, Winters and a handful of Easy men bluff a defence of the town.

q.t: How did Winters's small group hold Uden?
o: By bluffing strength they did not have
q.x: Cut off on 22 September, the group held the town for a day with a handful of men, bluffing strength they did not have.

d1-9.rem: For a day a handful of Easy men held Uden by bluffing strength they did not have.
d1-9.st: Winters and part of Easy Company moved to Uden while the rest of the battalion was still at Veghel. On 22 September the Germans cut the road between the two towns, and for a day the group in Uden held the town with a handful of men, bluffing strength they did not have until the road was reopened. Today the market square remains, with the corridor road running through it.

d1-10.ev: The Germans cut Hell's Highway for a day; burnt-out convoys line the road.

q.t: What was happening at Arnhem while the road here was cut?
o: The Poles were landing at Grave
q.x: The last cut of Hell's Highway came on 24–25 September; burnt-out convoys lined the road here while Arnhem fell.

d1-10.rem: The last cut of Hell's Highway: while the road was shut here, Arnhem fell.
d1-10.st: Koevering saw the last cut of Hell's Highway, on 24–25 September, on the straight road between Sint-Oedenrode and Veghel. The Germans closed the road for a day, and the 101st fought to reopen it while burnt-out convoys lined the way. Every hour the road was shut, the men at Arnhem were nearer defeat, and in these days Arnhem fell. Today the road itself is the exhibit, best driven slowly.

d2-1.ev: The 504th takes the Maas bridge intact within minutes of landing.

q.t: What was special about the Grave bridge?
o: It is the Arnhem road bridge
It was the first Market Garden bridge secured
q.x: The 504th took it intact within minutes of landing on 17 September, the first Market Garden bridge secured.

d2-1.rem: The 82nd's textbook success: the Maas bridge taken intact within minutes, in contrast to Son.
d2-1.st: The Maas bridge at Grave, now the John S. Thompson bridge, was taken intact by the 504th within minutes of landing on 17 September. It was the first Market Garden bridge secured, a textbook success for the 82nd Airborne. It stood in sharp contrast with Son, where the Germans blew the canal bridge in front of the 506th that same afternoon. Today the bridge still carries the road across the Maas.

d2-2.ev: The 504th crosses the Waal in canvas boats under fire as the Guards' tanks rush the bridge.

q.t: How did the 504th cross the Waal on 20 September?
o: By parachute on the north bank
q.x: The 504th crossed in canvas boats under fire and lost half of them, while the Guards' tanks rushed the road bridge, which fell at 19:00.

d2-2.rem: The width of the river is the story: half the boats were lost crossing it.
d2-2.st: On 20 September the 504th crossed the Waal in canvas boats under fire while the Guards' tanks rushed the road bridge at Nijmegen. Half the boats were lost, and the bridge fell at 19:00. It was an 82nd Airborne action, part of the same corridor plan in which Easy Company fought on Hell's Highway. Today the Waal crossing memorial stands on the south bank, where the width of the river tells the story.

d2-3.ev: The Market Garden and Rhineland story is told on the 82nd's landing ground.

q.t: Where does the Freedom Museum stand?
q.x: It stands on the 82nd's landing ground above Nijmegen and tells the whole Market Garden and Rhineland story.

d2-3.rem: The corridor map here places Easy's stretch of road inside the whole Market Garden plan.
d2-3.st: The Freedom Museum at Groesbeek stands on the 82nd Airborne's landing ground above Nijmegen. It tells the whole Market Garden and Rhineland story, from the airborne landings to the fighting that followed. Easy Company's war on Hell's Highway and later on the Island was one thread of that larger plan. Today the corridor map is the most useful exhibit, placing Easy's road inside the whole design.

d2-4.ev: Sosabowski's Poles land and try to reach the trapped British across the river.

q.t: What were the Polish paratroopers trying to do at Driel?
o: Reach the trapped British across the river
q.x: Sosabowski's Poles landed on 21 September and tried to reach the trapped British across the river.

d2-4.rem: The Island begins here, looking north across the Rhine to Oosterbeek, where the British were trapped.
d2-4.st: On 21 September Sosabowski's Poles landed at Driel and tried to reach the trapped British across the river. Driel marks the start of the Island, the flat polder between the Waal and the Neder-Rijn. In October, after Market Garden failed at Arnhem, the 101st relieved the British on the Island, and Easy Company would spend weeks on its dikes. Today the view runs north across the Rhine to Oosterbeek.

d2-5.ev: Winters's bayonet-led attack at first light breaks a larger SS force at the junction.
d2-5.rem: This was Winters's last fight as company commander; the memorial names Pvt. William Dukeman, Easy's one man killed.
d2-5.st: At dawn on 5 October 1944, at this junction on the Randwijkse Rijndijk, Winters took a squad, then a platoon, against a much larger German force, which he estimated at two SS companies. A bayonet-led assault and a covering line of machine guns broke it: about 50 killed and 11 captured, for one Easy man killed and 22 wounded. The memorial names that man, Pvt. William Dukeman. Today the whole action fits in the view from the dike.

d2-6.ev: About 138 Allied evaders, mostly British, are rowed across the Neder-Rijn with Easy covering.

q.t: What was Easy's role in Operation Pegasus?
o: Covering force on the south bank
q.x: Easy covered the south bank while the 506th brought about 138 evaders across in boats; Lt. Heyliger led the crossing party.

d2-6.rem: About 138 Allied evaders from Arnhem, mostly British, came back across this river in a single night.
d2-6.st: On the night of 22–23 October 1944, about 138 Allied evaders from Arnhem, mostly British, were brought across the Neder-Rijn in boats by the 506th. Easy Company provided the covering force on this south bank, and Lt. Heyliger, now commanding Easy, led the crossing party. It was a quiet success in the weeks after the failure at Arnhem. Today the far bank is Renkum, whose woods hid the escapers.

d2-7.ev: Frost's 700 men, after holding the north end for four days, are overrun.

q.t: How long did Frost's men hold the north end of the bridge?
q.x: Frost's 700 men held the north end for four days and were overrun on 21 September. The rebuilt bridge carries his name.

d2-7.rem: A bridge too far: the rebuilt bridge carries the name of the commander whose men held it for four days.
d2-7.st: At Arnhem, the bridge too far, Frost's 700 men held the north end of the bridge for four days before they were overrun on 21 September. They were the men the whole corridor, including Easy Company's stretch of Hell's Highway, was trying to reach. The rebuilt bridge now carries Frost's name. Today the visitor can stand at the north end, on the side where the paratroopers held the houses.

d2-8.ev: Urquhart's HQ holds a perimeter for nine days before Operation Berlin's night evacuation.

q.t: What was the Hartenstein hotel during the battle?
q.x: It was Urquhart's headquarters; after nine days in the perimeter came Operation Berlin, the night evacuation to the river.

d2-8.rem: The evacuation ran south to the same river Easy watched from the other side a month later.
d2-8.st: The Hartenstein hotel was Urquhart's headquarters during the Arnhem battle and is now its museum. The British held their perimeter for nine days before Operation Berlin's night evacuation took them back across the river. A month later Easy Company watched that same river from the other bank, during Operation Pegasus. Today the museum marks the start of the evacuation route, which ran south from here to the water.

d2-9.ev: The dead of the 1st Airborne Division's battle at Arnhem are buried here.
d2-9.rem: 1,700 graves, mostly of the 1st Airborne Division; local schoolchildren lay flowers here every September.
d2-9.st: The Airborne War Cemetery at Oosterbeek holds 1,700 graves, most of them men of the 1st Airborne Division from the Arnhem battle. They were the soldiers the corridor, and Easy Company's part in it, was meant to reach. Every September local schoolchildren lay flowers on the graves, a remembrance carried on by each new generation. Today it is a quiet place to end the day.

d3-1.ev: The 101st holds encircled Bastogne through the siege of the Battle of the Bulge.

q.t: What lies on the skyline north-east of the Mardasson?
q.x: From the Mardasson the Bois Jacques is the dark line on the north-east skyline, where Easy held its line.

d3-1.rem: The best single museum of the Bulge stands beside the star-shaped American memorial; it gives the siege its shape.
d3-1.st: The 101st arrived at Bastogne on the night of 18–19 December 1944 and was encircled from 21 December. The Bastogne War Museum, beside the star-shaped Mardasson Memorial, is the best single museum of the Bulge and gives the siege its shape before a visit to the woods where Easy Company held its line. Today, from the Mardasson, the Bois Jacques shows as a dark line on the north-east skyline.

d3-2.ev: The 506th holds its right-hand village on the road to the Easy positions.

q.t: What runs from Bizory to Foy?
q.x: Bizory was the 506th's right-hand village; the road from here to Foy runs straight through the Easy Company positions.

d3-2.rem: The road north from here to Foy runs straight through the Easy Company positions.
d3-2.st: Bizory was the 506th's right-hand village in the defence of Bastogne. The road from here to Foy runs straight through the Easy Company positions in the Bois Jacques, where the company dug in from 19 December and held through fog, snow and shelling. It is the natural gateway to Easy's ground in the Ardennes. Today the route turns north here onto the Foy road.

d3-3.ev: Fourteen Easy men are killed in these woods between 18 December and 13 January.
d3-3.rem: Fourteen names of Easy men killed here are listed beside a text about −28 °C nights with little food and ammunition.
d3-3.st: The Men of Easy Company Foundation built this memorial on the Bizory–Foy road. It carries fourteen names of Easy men killed here between 18 December and 13 January, and a text recalling −28 °C nights with little food and ammunition. Encircled and without winter gear, the company held this line through fog, snow and shelling. Today the visitor reads the names and then walks on into the wood.

d3-4.ev: Encircled, Easy holds its foxhole line on the edge of the Bois Jacques above Foy.

q.t: What made the shelling in these woods so deadly?
q.x: Tree bursts made the wood itself the weapon; on 3 January Joe Toye and Bill Guarnere each lost a leg.

d3-4.rem: Easy held this line encircled, without winter gear or enough ammunition, through fog, snow and shelling.
d3-4.st: From 19 December Easy Company dug in on the edge of the Bois Jacques, looking down on Foy, and held here through the siege. On 3 January German artillery caught the company in the trees: Joe Toye and Bill Guarnere each lost a leg, and tree bursts made the wood itself the weapon. The foxholes survive on both sides of the road, shallower now but unmistakable. Today a paid, app-guided walk with numbered markers leads through them.

d3-5.ev: Easy attacks across open snow; Speirs relieves Dike and runs through the village.

q.t: Whom did Winters send to take over the attack on Foy?
q.x: When Lt. Dike's advance stopped in the open, Winters sent Ronald Speirs, who ran through the village to link up with I Company and back.

d3-5.rem: From the church, look back to the wood-line: 250 m of open snow that Easy crossed to take Foy.
d3-5.st: On 13 January 1945 Easy Company attacked across the open snow into Foy. Lt. Dike's advance stopped in the open, and Winters, watching from the wood-line, sent Ronald Speirs to relieve him; Speirs ran through the village to link up with I Company and back again. Foy fell, and Shifty Powers shot the German sniper who had done much of the damage. Today, from the church, the slope up to the wood-line shows 250 m of nothing.

d3-6.ev: The 506th pushes north from Foy, and Easy takes Noville on 15 January.

q.t: Who held Noville on 19–20 December?
q.x: Team Desobry of the 10th Armored held Noville on 19–20 December; the 506th took it on 14–15 January.

d3-6.rem: Noville saw two stands a month apart: Team Desobry's in December and the 506th's attack in January.
d3-6.st: Noville was held by the 10th Armored's Team Desobry on 19–20 December, at the start of the siege. Less than a month later it became the 506th's objective as the regiment pushed north from Foy, and Easy took the village on 15 January, the day the US 1st and 3rd Armies were about to meet at Houffalize and close the Bulge. Today a small museum and memorials stand near the crossroads and church.

d3-7.ev: Easy takes its last Ardennes objective and spends the night in the church.

q.t: What happened in the Rachamps church after Easy's last attack?
o: They handed over to the British
q.x: The company slept in the church, where the village schoolgirls sang for them; the 101st was relieved the next day.

d3-7.rem: Bastogne cost Easy fourteen killed, about 32 wounded and 21 evacuated for cold-weather injuries; its memorial stands beside this church.
d3-7.st: Rachamps was Easy Company's last objective in the Ardennes, reached on 16 January 1945. The company spent the night in the church, where the village schoolgirls sang for them. On 17 January the 101st was relieved; Bastogne had cost Easy fourteen killed, about 32 wounded and 21 evacuated for cold-weather injuries. Today a memorial stands beside the church, with a tree planted by Guarnere and Heffron.

d3-8.ev: German dead of the Bulge are buried a kilometre from Foy.
d3-8.rem: 6,800 German dead from the Bulge rest here, the men on the other side of the snowfield.
d3-8.st: The Recogne German war cemetery holds 6,800 German dead from the Bulge. It lies about a kilometre from Foy, where Easy Company attacked across the snow in January 1945. These were the men on the other side of the snowfield, and their graves complete the story told in the woods nearby. Today it is, before anything else, a place of remembrance.

d4-1.ev: The siege of Bastogne is told through a strong 101st collection in the old officers' mess.

q.t: What building houses the 101st Airborne Museum?
q.x: The museum is in the former officers' mess, with uniforms, a bomb-shelter experience and a strong 101st collection.

d4-1.rem: Its bomb-shelter experience conveys the human scale of the siege.
d4-1.st: The 101st Airborne Museum occupies the former officers' mess at Avenue de la Gare 11 in Bastogne. It tells the story of the siege through uniforms, a bomb-shelter experience and a strong 101st collection. Here the men who held the town, Easy Company among them, are seen at close range rather than on a map. Today the museum is especially good for the human scale of the siege.

d4-2.ev: McAuliffe's staff answer the German surrender demand with 'Nuts!'.

q.t: How was the German surrender demand answered on 22 December?
q.x: In these barracks, where General McAuliffe's staff worked in the cellars, the German surrender demand was answered with 'Nuts!' on 22 December.

d4-2.rem: The cellars where McAuliffe's staff worked, and where the demand was answered with 'Nuts!', are the real thing.
d4-2.st: During the siege General McAuliffe's staff worked in the cellars of these Belgian barracks. It was here, on 22 December 1944, that the German demand for surrender was answered with the single word 'Nuts'. Out in the Bois Jacques, Easy Company was holding its line at the time, encircled since 21 December. Today guided visits lead through the real cellar and a large vehicle restoration hall.

d4-3.ev: Seven roads meet at this square, the reason the 101st is sent to Bastogne.

q.t: Why was the 101st sent to Bastogne?
q.x: The square sits at the centre of the seven roads, the reason the 101st was sent here.

d4-3.rem: Count the roads: seven meet here, and that is why the 101st was sent to Bastogne.
d4-3.st: Bastogne mattered because seven roads met at its centre, and that is why the 101st was sent here in December 1944. The square at the heart of that junction now carries General McAuliffe's name, and a Sherman tank knocked out at Renuamont stands beside his bust. Easy Company's line in the Bois Jacques lay out beyond it. Today the visitor can count the roads leaving the square and see the reason for the siege.

d4-4.ev: The US 1st and 3rd Armies meet here to close the Bulge.

q.t: What happened at Houffalize on 16 January?
q.x: The US 1st and 3rd Armies met here on 16 January to close the Bulge, the same day Easy took Rachamps.

d4-4.rem: The Bulge was closed here on the same day Easy took Rachamps, 10 km to the south.
d4-4.st: On 16 January 1945 the US 1st and 3rd Armies met at Houffalize and closed the Bulge. On the same day Easy Company took Rachamps, 10 km to the south, its final objective in the Ardennes. The meeting brought to an end the German offensive that had sent the 101st to Bastogne a month before. Today a German Panther tank sits in the town centre.

d4-5.ev: Kampfgruppe Peiper reaches its high-water mark on the northern shoulder.

q.t: What tank stands outside the December 44 Museum?
q.x: A King Tiger stands outside, at the high-water mark of Kampfgruppe Peiper on the northern shoulder.

d4-5.rem: This is the German side of the offensive: the furthest point Kampfgruppe Peiper reached.
d4-5.st: La Gleize marked the high-water mark of Kampfgruppe Peiper on the northern shoulder of the German offensive, the farthest point its advance reached there. The December 44 Museum tells that story from the German side, a counterpoint to the American defence at Bastogne, where Easy Company held the line in the Bois Jacques. Today a King Tiger tank stands outside the museum.

d4-6.ev: 84 American prisoners are shot at the Baugnez crossroads.
d4-6.rem: 84 American prisoners were shot here; the memorial wall and the field remain open as a place of remembrance.
d4-6.st: At the Baugnez crossroads, on 17 December 1944, 84 American prisoners were shot. It was the same day the German offensive in the Ardennes changed everything for the 101st, which was alerted that night at Mourmelon. The Baugnez 44 Historical Center beside the crossroads closed permanently in January 2023. Today the memorial wall and the field remain open, and this is a place of remembrance first.

d5-1.ev: The 506th holds the Moder line in deep snow as Operation Nordwind ends.

q.t: What was the 506th's task along the Moder?
o: Holding the line in deep snow
q.x: The 506th held sectors of the Moder valley west of Haguenau in deep snow, mostly patrolling and being shelled, as Nordwind ended.

d5-1.rem: Nordwind was the last German offensive in the west; the 506th held this line in deep snow as it ended.
d5-1.st: In late January 1945 the 101st moved to Alsace as Operation Nordwind, the last German offensive in the west, was ending. The 506th held sectors of the Moder valley west of Haguenau in deep snow, mostly patrolling and being shelled. These villages along the river, Pfaffenhoffen among them, were part of that line. Today the river road east toward Haguenau follows the same valley.

d5-2.ev: Lt. Jones's patrol crosses the Moder and brings back two prisoners from a German outpost.

q.t: How far apart were Easy and the Germans in Haguenau?
q.x: Easy held the south bank inside the town with the Germans a street away; the 15 February patrol crossed somewhere here.

d5-2.rem: Eugene Jackson was mortally wounded on the 15 February patrol; Haguenau was the company's last combat.
d5-2.st: From 5 to 23 February 1945 Easy Company held the south bank of the Moder inside Haguenau, with the Germans a street away on the north bank. On the night of 15 February a patrol led by Lt. Jones crossed somewhere here, blew into a German outpost and brought back two prisoners; Eugene Jackson was mortally wounded in the fight. Winters quietly cancelled the second patrol ordered for the next night. Today the river is the width of a street.

d5-3.ev: American tanks cross the Moder canal for Haguenau's final liberation.

q.t: When did Haguenau's final liberation come, relative to Easy's stay?
q.x: American tanks crossed the Moder canal on 16 March 1945, three weeks after Easy left the town.

d5-3.rem: The town's final liberation came on 16 March 1945, three weeks after Easy left.
d5-3.st: On 16 March 1945 American tanks crossed the Moder canal at this spot on Boulevard de la Libération, bringing Haguenau its final liberation. By then Easy Company had been gone for three weeks, relieved on 23 February after holding the river front inside the town. The memorial marks the end of the long standoff across the water. Today its bronze reliefs show the crossing.

d5-4.ev: Easy holds a half-ruined front-line town, with the Germans across the river.

q.t: How did Easy know Haguenau?
q.x: Easy knew the old Alsatian town as a half-ruined front line; the museum covers its two liberations of 1944–45.

d5-4.rem: The intact streets today stand in contrast to the shelled town Easy knew in February 1945.
d5-4.st: In February 1945 Easy Company knew Haguenau as a half-ruined front line, with the Germans holding the far bank of the Moder, and it was here that the company saw its last combat. The old Alsatian town has since recovered, and the Musée Historique covers its two liberations of 1944–45. Today the intact streets invite comparison with the shelled town the men saw.

d5-5.ev: The 1945 winter fighting runs along the fortified border this Maginot fort guarded.

q.t: What is Fort de Schoenenbourg?
o: The largest visitable Maginot fort in Alsace
q.x: It is the largest visitable Maginot fort in Alsace, with kilometres of galleries and turrets, 20 km north of Haguenau.

d5-5.rem: Its kilometres of galleries and turrets show the fortified border on which the 1945 winter fighting sat.
d5-5.st: Fort de Schoenenbourg, 20 km north of Haguenau, is the largest visitable Maginot fort in Alsace, with kilometres of galleries and turrets. It gives context for the fortified border on which the winter fighting of 1945 took place, including Easy Company's weeks on the Moder. The fort shows how the border had been prepared for war long before. Today the galleries stay at 12 °C underground, so a jacket is worth bringing.

x-jm.ev: Pvt. Joe Mann of the 502nd throws himself on a grenade in the Best bridge fight.

q.t: What did Pvt. Joe Mann do at Best?
q.x: Joe Mann of the 502nd threw himself on a grenade at the Best bridge fight on 19 September and received the Medal of Honor.

x-jm.rem: Pvt. Joe Mann received the Medal of Honor for throwing himself on a grenade in the woods where the 502nd fought.
x-jm.st: During the fight at the Best bridge on 19 September 1944, Pvt. Joe Mann of the 502nd threw himself on a grenade. He was awarded the Medal of Honor. The action was part of the 101st's struggle to hold the Market Garden corridor in the days after the landings. Today the pelican memorial stands in the woods where the 502nd fought, ten minutes from the Wings of Liberation museum.

x-elst.ev: The 506th holds Elst and its sector of the Island through the autumn.

q.t: Where is Elst?
q.x: Elst is on the Island, the town the 506th held in October and November 1944.

x-elst.rem: The 506th held this town on the Island through October and November 1944.
x-elst.st: In October and November 1944 the 506th held the town of Elst on the Island, the flat polder between the Waal and the Neder-Rijn. It was a static war of outposts on the dike, night patrols across the flooded polder, German artillery, rain and cold, which Easy Company endured for seven weeks. The memorial here honours the regiment. Today it lies on the way from Driel to the Heteren crossroads.

x-mou.ev: The 101st refits here until the Ardennes offensive alerts it on 17 December.

q.t: What interrupted the 101st's refit at Mourmelon?
o: The German offensive in the Ardennes
q.x: The division refitted here between Holland and Bastogne; on 17 December the German offensive in the Ardennes changed everything.

x-mou.rem: The garrison town where the 101st refitted between Holland and Bastogne, and where Easy returned after Haguenau.
x-mou.st: Mourmelon-le-Grand was the Champagne garrison town where the 101st refitted between Holland and Bastogne. In its old French army barracks came replacements, passes to Paris and football, and a company that expected to spend the winter there, until the German offensive in the Ardennes brought an alert on the night of 17 December. Easy returned here after Haguenau. Today it is still a French army camp, two hours west of Bastogne.

dd-0.ev: A tank battle is fought here, east of the Market Garden corridor.

q.t: What happened at Overloon in October 1944?
q.x: Overloon was the site of the October 1944 tank battle east of the corridor; the museum has one of Europe's largest vehicle collections.

dd-0.rem: One of the largest vehicle collections in Europe stands on the ground of the October 1944 tank battle.
dd-0.st: In October 1944 a tank battle was fought at Overloon, east of the Market Garden corridor, in the aftermath of the operation Easy Company had jumped into. The Overloon War Museum now stands on the site of that battle. It holds one of the largest vehicle collections in Europe, and its scale suits the armoured fighting it recalls. Today its big halls reward a visit of about two hours.

dd-1.ev: American dead of Holland, the Bulge and the Rhineland are buried here.
dd-1.rem: Among the 8,300 graves are 101st men who fell in Holland, the Bulge and the Rhineland.
dd-1.st: The Netherlands American Cemetery at Margraten holds about 8,300 graves of Americans who died in Holland, the Bulge and the Rhineland. Among them are men of the 101st, the division with which Easy Company fought on Hell's Highway and at Bastogne. Their graves bring the story of the corridor and the siege back to individual lives. Today the cemetery lies between the Dutch and Belgian legs of the tour.

dd-2.ev: American dead of the Bulge and the Rhineland are buried north of Liège.
dd-2.rem: 7,900 graves hold American dead of the Bulge and the Rhineland.
dd-2.st: The Henri-Chapelle American Cemetery, north of Liège, holds about 7,900 graves of Americans who died in the Bulge and the Rhineland. Many fell in the same campaign in which Easy Company held the Bois Jacques outside Bastogne. It is a place for quiet remembrance, set apart from the battlefields themselves. Today it lies on the way to the northern shoulder of the Bulge.

dd-3.ev: The 2nd and 99th Divisions stop the 6th Panzer Army on the northern shoulder.

q.t: Which divisions held Elsenborn Ridge?
q.x: The 2nd and 99th Divisions stopped the 6th Panzer Army here, the shoulder that held.

dd-3.rem: The northern shoulder of the Bulge held here, stopping the 6th Panzer Army.
dd-3.st: On Elsenborn Ridge the 2nd and 99th Divisions stopped the 6th Panzer Army on the northern shoulder of the Bulge. It was the shoulder that held, while to the south the 101st and Easy Company were encircled at Bastogne. The two stands belong to the same December battle. Today the ridge is open ground, with memorials at Rocherath-Krinkelt.

dd-4.ev: The 110th Infantry holds the castle for two days, delaying Panzer Lehr.

q.t: Why did the stand at Clervaux matter to Bastogne?
o: It delayed Panzer Lehr on the road there
q.x: The 110th Infantry held the castle for two days, 16–18 December, delaying Panzer Lehr on the road to Bastogne.

dd-4.rem: Two days held at Clervaux bought time on the road to Bastogne.
dd-4.st: In Luxembourg the castle at Clervaux was held for two days, 16–18 December 1944, by the 110th Infantry. That stand delayed Panzer Lehr on the road to Bastogne, where the 101st, Easy Company among it, arrived on the night of 18–19 December after ten hours in open trucks. Clervaux lay on that road, and every hour mattered. Today a museum occupies the castle.

dd-5.ev: The Third Army's dead of the Bulge are buried here with their general.
dd-5.rem: The Third Army's dead of the Bulge lie here, 5,000 graves, with General Patton among them.
dd-5.st: The Luxembourg American Cemetery at Hamm holds about 5,000 graves, the Third Army's dead of the Bulge, and their general, Patton, lies among them. It was Patton's 4th Armored Division that broke through to Bastogne on 26 December 1944, reaching the encircled 101st and Easy Company in the Bois Jacques. Today the cemetery lies quietly at Hamm, outside Luxembourg city.

dd-6.ev: The only Nazi camp on French soil is liberated.
dd-6.rem: The only Nazi camp on French soil, liberated in November 1944, is now a memorial site in the Vosges.
dd-6.st: Natzweiler-Struthof was the only Nazi camp on French soil. It was liberated in November 1944, some two months before the 101st came to Alsace to hold the Moder line in the snow. It belongs to the same Alsace in which Easy Company fought its last battles. Today the memorial site in the Vosges is a place for quiet remembrance.
